item.title: Cubs To Sign Teruaki Sato
item.dc:creator: Charlie Wright
item.description: The Cubs have agreed to a six-year, $120MM deal with slugger Teruaki Sato. He’s expected to play a corner outfield spot in Chicago. Sato is represented by VC Sports Group. Chicago has dropped $240MM in the span of 12 hours on two massive additions. The club signed left-hander Trevor Rogers last night, and now locks […]
item.content:encoded:
The Cubs have agreed to a six-year, $120MM deal with slugger Teruaki Sato. He’s expected to play a corner outfield spot in Chicago. Sato is represented by VC Sports Group.

Chicago has dropped $240MM in the span of 12 hours on two massive additions. The club signed left-hander Trevor Rogers last night, and now locks up one of the top bats in the free agent market. Sato won the Triple Crown in NPB last season, slashing .306/.383/.609 with 39 home runs.

The 27-year-old Sato has mostly played third base with the Hanshin Tigers, but he does have experience in the outfield. He’s made 44 starts in right field over the past two seasons. The Cubs entered the offseason with multiple voids to fill alongside Pete Crow-Armstrong with longtime outfielders Seiya Suzuki and Ian Happ hitting free agency.

Suzuki and Randy Arozarena were the only hitters ranked above Sato in our Top 50 Free Agents list. The two-time Central League MVP has taken his game to another level over the past two years, piling up 79 homers and 208 RBI. He scored 100 runs for the first time in his career this past season. Sato has had a strikeout rate around 27% in each of the last three seasons. The swing-and-miss is the main concern as he transitions to MLB, though the issue isn’t as severe as it was for fellow NPB import Munetaka Murakami, who was able to hit the ground running with the White Sox.

Sato will join the top offense in the game. The Cubs comfortably paced the league in scoring this past season. His addition, plus the losses of Suzuki and Happ, will shift the balance of the lineup. The lefty-swinging Sato will replace a right-handed bat in Suzuki. He should be near the top of the order with fellow lefties Crow-Armstrong and Michael Busch. Righties Alex Bregman and Nico Hoerner likely slot somewhere between the lefty contingent.

The final cost will be more than the reported $120MM. Chicago will also owe a posting fee to Hanshin. Based on the size of Sato’s deal, the number heading to the Tigers will be around $20MM.

The internal replacements for Suzuki and Happ include Pedro Ramirez, Matt Shaw, and Kevin Alcantara. With Sato aboard, the Cubs will have to lean on that trio for just one spot in the outfield. The club could also look for another addition. Shaw got a brief look as the everyday right fielder to begin 2026 with Suzuki tending to an injury. He faded to a backup role once Suzuki was healthy. Ramirez was solid in his first taste of the majors, but the majority of his opportunities came in the infield. He spent a total of one inning on the grass.

The Cubs also need to fill at-bats at DH. The team rotated through options at that spot, with no player getting more than 170 plate appearances there. Suzuki, Michael Conforto, and Moises Ballesteros led the roster in DH reps. None of them are in Chicago anymore.

The Blue Jays, Padres, Phillies, Diamondbacks, Yankees, Rangers, and Tigers were known to have at least some level of interest in Sato. Those teams will have to head back to the drawing board to find an impact bat. Suzuki and Arozarena are the top prizes left. Brandon Lowe, Luis Arraez, Jazz Chisholm Jr., and Happ are in the next tier. The corner infield market is relatively thin beyond Ty France. Alec Bohm, Mauricio Dubon, and Rhys Hoskins are among the top remaining options for teams.

Michael Cerami of Bleacher Nation first reported the Cubs and Sato were finalizing a deal. Jeff Passan of ESPN was first on the financial terms. Passan also noted that Sato would play corner outfield in Chicago.

Photos courtesy of Darren Yamashita, Imagn Images

item.title: Orioles Sign Freddy Peralta
item.dc:creator: Anthony Franco
item.description: The Orioles announced the signing of free agent starter Freddy Peralta to a five-year contract. It’s reportedly a $125MM guarantee that takes the form of a $10MM signing bonus followed by $23MM annual salaries from 2027-31. The deal does not contain any deferred money or opt-outs. Peralta, an ACES client, was traded from the Mets to […]
item.content:encoded:
The Orioles announced the signing of free agent starter Freddy Peralta to a five-year contract. It’s reportedly a $125MM guarantee that takes the form of a $10MM signing bonus followed by $23MM annual salaries from 2027-31. The deal does not contain any deferred money or opt-outs. Peralta, an ACES client, was traded from the Mets to the Rays midseason and thus was ineligible to receive a qualifying offer.

Peralta lands in Baltimore one day after they watched Trevor Rogers depart for Chicago. The two pitchers end up in a similar place contractually, as Rogers also signed for five years at a slightly lower $120MM guarantee. The O’s picked up a compensatory draft choice after the first round next summer as a result of Rogers’ departure. Peralta doesn’t cost Baltimore any form of draft compensation.

It turns out to be a fairly direct replacement for Baltimore president of baseball operations Mike Elias. It’s not necessarily the case that the O’s chose Peralta and the draft choice over Rogers — the players could have geographical or team fit preferences — but the similar contracts will make their career arcs an intriguing subplot over the next half-decade.

Peralta has had a wildly up-and-down last 12 months. He finished fifth in NL Cy Young balloting in 2025, posting a career-low 2.70 earned run average across 33 starts for Milwaukee. The Brewers, who were highly unlikely to sign him long term, traded him to the Mets last offseason. Spring Training extension talks didn’t progress, seemingly because of a hangup between the club and pitcher on contract length.

Three months later, Peralta was back on the trade block. The Mets had a nightmare season, partially because Peralta had such a disappointing tenure in Queens. He allowed just under 5.00 earned runs per nine innings across 22 starts in a Mets uniform. His strikeout rate dropped six percentage points relative to his final season in Milwaukee. He allowed a few more home runs and had a difficult time stranding runners. New York’s lackluster defense didn’t do him any favors either, but Peralta clearly wasn’t performing at the same caliber as he did with the Brewers.

The Rays acquired Peralta for three prospects at the deadline. His fortunes turned around in Tampa Bay. The two-time All-Star fired 55 1/3 innings of 3.25 ERA ball in the regular season. He added another 21 1/3 frames with a 2.95 mark in the postseason, helping the Rays to a World Series berth.

Although the late-season run prevention looked much like the Peralta of old, he didn’t return to missing bats the way he had in Milwaukee. He struck out fewer than 20% of hitters with the Rays in the regular season and posted an unimpressive 16:10 strikeout-to-walk ratio in October. Peralta’s turnaround was attributable more to a swing in his batted ball results. Opposing hitters had batted .313 on balls in play while he was with the Mets; his BABIP against dropped to .232 for Tampa Bay.

A lot of that is beyond a pitcher’s control, the product of team defense and batted ball variance. However, it’s not fair to chalk up Peralta’s late-season results entirely to his teammates and better luck. He made a significant repertoire adjustment, scaling up the use of his changeup in Tampa Bay — a trait shared by a lot of Rays’ pitchers this year. Peralta’s average fastball velocity ticked up from 94 to 95 mph late in the season and climbed near 97 in the playoffs. He’s not going to sit at 97 for an entire regular season, as that’s mostly a product of adrenaline and the expectation of shorter starts, but Peralta’s velocity was every bit as strong as it had been in Milwaukee.

The end result was a 4.42 ERA with league average strikeout and walk rates (21.4% and 8.6%, respectively) over 169 innings. It’s a clear step back from the 3.40 ERA and 29% strikeout percentage he posted over the previous three years. That’s reflected in the price, as Peralta entered the year with an argument for a $200MM+ contract that placed him alongside the likes of Max Fried and Dylan Cease. His first-half performance pointed toward a potential pillow contract, but his late-season rebound allowed him to land between Rogers and Ranger Suarez (five years and $130MM). He’s being paid as a #2 caliber starter.

Peralta brings a sterling durability track record to Baltimore. He hasn’t gone on the injured list since 2022 and is one of two pitchers (along with Kevin Gausman) to start 30+ games in each of the past four seasons. Peralta joins Kyle Bradish and Shane Baz in the upper half of Craig Albernaz’s rotation. That pushes Brandon Young to the role of #4 starter and leaves a competition for the final spot among Trey Gibson, Cade Povich and a crop of talented upper minors prospects that includes Michael Forret, Nestor German, Luis De León and eventually Anthony Eyanson.

The Orioles have built some decent rotation depth but may still lack a true #1 starter. Tarik Skubal was the only one available in free agency, and the O’s never seemed likely to compete with the Mets on a $400MM+ deal for him. Peralta was in the mix for the second-best free agent arm available. The O’s could still look to the trade market for a higher-ceiling arm (e.g. Reid Detmers, Logan Webb), potentially consolidating some of their rotation prospects in such a move.

As shown on MLBTR’s Payroll Tracker, the Orioles entered the day with a projected 2027 payroll around $127MM. They opened the 2026 season north of $160MM, so they should have room for another mid-level salary or two even after adding Peralta’s $25MM average annual value to the books. Baltimore has broadly been open to reshuffling much of the roster. They should be in the market for a corner outfielder and have kicked around adding a bat behind the plate to split time with Samuel Basallo between catcher and designated hitter.

Héctor Gómez of Z101 first reported the Orioles and Peralta were discussing a five-year, $125MM contract. Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic confirmed the agreement and noted the absence of deferrals or opt-outs. Noah Trister of The Associated Press reported the signing bonus. Image courtesy of Nathan Ray Seebeck, Imagn Images.

item.title: Blue Jays To Sign Kaima Taira
item.dc:creator: Darragh McDonald
item.description: The Blue Jays and right-hander Kaima Taira have reportedly agreed to a five-year, $80MM deal. There’s an opt-out after the third year and a $5MM signing bonus for the Boras Corporation client. The Jays will also owe a posting fee of $13.875MM to the Seibu Lions, Taira’s NPB team which posted him earlier this month, […]
item.content:encoded:
The Blue Jays and right-hander Kaima Taira have reportedly agreed to a five-year, $80MM deal. There’s an opt-out after the third year and a $5MM signing bonus for the Boras Corporation client. The Jays will also owe a posting fee of $13.875MM to the Seibu Lions, Taira’s NPB team which posted him earlier this month, so they are spending $93.875MM in total. The Jays have an open 40-man spot and won’t need to make a corresponding move.

Taira, 27, comes to North America with intriguing stuff but some unusual aspects to his profile. With the Lions, he broke in as a reliever and had a lot of success in that role. From 2020 to 2022, he finished each season with at least 53 innings pitched and an earned run average under 2.00. He got stretched out in 2023 and fared well. He made 23 starts and logged 150 innings with a 2.40 ERA, 25% strikeout rate, 9% walk rate and 46.2% ground ball rate.

That seemingly established him as a viable starter but he hit some snags from there. Injuries limited him in 2024, so he was kept in relief that season and the subsequent campaign as well. The results were still good, with an ERA under 2.00 in both of those seasons, so the Lions stretched him out again in 2026. He seemed to make the move back to the rotation without issue, logging 146 innings this year with a 1.36 ERA, 24.8% strikeout rate, 7.9% walk rate and 48.5% ground ball rate.

One could look at that trajectory and point out that Taira only has two seasons of experience as a starter, which weren’t even consecutive. There’s some risk in there but the arsenal is tantalizing. He has upper-90s velocity on his fastball and can hold it deep into games, according to scouts who spoke to MLBTR. He also throws a splitter, cutter and slider.

Taira’s build is also a talking point, as he is listed at 5’8″ and about 220 pounds, a frame that has been compared to catchers such as a Alejandro Kirk. Amusingly, it now seems that Taira and Kirk will be forming a battery together in Toronto. There’s not a huge track record of starting pitchers finding success at this size, though Blue Jays fans are surely aware that 5’7″ Marcus Stroman did plenty of good work in the majors.

It seems that the Blue Jays and several other clubs feel there’s a good chance Taira, like Stroman, can break the mold and find success in a big league rotation despite a lack of height. MLBTR predicted Taira for a four-year, $72MM deal. He was connected to teams such as the Cubs, White Sox, Mets, Padres and Tigers. The Jays got a deal done by going a bit beyond MLBTR’s prediction by adding an extra year, though at a slightly lower average annual value. Even if he doesn’t stick in a rotation, he has plenty of experience in the bullpen and should have that as a fallback.

The rotation market has been moving fast and the Jays have clearly been in the mix there. They reportedly made a $420MM offer to Tarik Skubal but got outbid when the Mets went to $450MM. The Jays were then connected to Trevor Rogers and Freddy Peralta but those two pitchers went to the Cubs and Orioles, respectively.

Last year, the Jays lost both José Berríos and Bowden Francis to Tommy John surgery. Further rotation injuries became an issue throughout the season, contributing to the club falling out of the race. At the summer deadline, they traded away impending free agent Kevin Gausman but also acquired controllable starters by getting José Soriano from the Angels and Spencer Arrighetti in a deal with the Astros. At season’s end, Max Scherzer and Shane Bieber became free agents.

Toronto went into the offseason with a projected rotation core of Dylan Cease, Trey Yesavage and Soriano. They had some options for the back-end spots, including Arrighetti, Cody Ponce, Chad Dallas and Jake Bloss. Once healthy, Francis and Berríos will be in the mix. The Jays clearly wanted to add to that group, based on their pursuits of Skubal, Rogers, Peralta and others.

Ideally, Taira will be a viable starter against big league hitters and will strengthen that group, bumping most of those arms down one peg on the depth chart. If Taira struggles in the rotation, then perhaps he will end up in a leverage relief role, but the price point of this deal suggests the Jays view him as a legit starter.

If Taira succeeds, he will have a chance to return to free agency three years from now with fewer question marks about his profile. At that time, he will be wrapping up his age-29 season and could be lined up for another strong multi-year deal. If the qualifying offer system still exists in the next collective bargaining agreement and he’s still with the Jays after 2029, the club would be in position to recoup a draft pick if he departs for another team. Of course, if he decides to stay with the Jays for 2030 and 2031, that means he hasn’t lived up to the contract in the first three years.

When a player is posted by his NPB team, that club is entitled to a posting fee, which is on top of the money going to the player. The fee is calculated based on the size of the guarantee, including 20% of the first $25MM, 17.5% of the next $25MM, and then 15% for anything beyond that. For a guarantee of $80MM, that works out to a posting fee of $13.875MM.

The Jays arguably opened the offseason with a greater need in the lineup but the rotation market has been moving fast ahead of the lockout, which is expected to start just over a week from now. Dustin May, Sonny Gray, Skubal, Rogers, Peralta and Kris Bubic have come off the board in the past week. For clubs looking for rotation help, Michael King, Tyler Mahle, Clay Holmes and Gausman are some of the top names still available.

With Taira in hand, the Jays will now likely focus on the position player group. The outfield corners and second base appear to be their targets, as they have been connected to players such as Seiya Suzuki, Randy Arozarena and Brandon Lowe.

MLBTR’s Payroll Tracker from contributor Ethan Hullihen projects the 2027 Blue Jays for a cash payroll of roughly $238MM and a competitive balance tax number of $233MM. Taira’s deal has an average annual value of $16MM, so he will add that amount to the CBT number, getting it near $250MM. With the ongoing CBA negotiations, it’s unclear where the tax brackets will be next year, or if that system will even be in place.

Taira’s impact on the cash payroll will depend upon the annual breakdown of the salaries. The Jays finished 2026 with a cash payroll of $276MM and a CBT calculation of $317MM. It’s unknown where they want to end up in 2027 but they should have some powder dry for at least one big bat.

Jon Heyman of The New York Post first reported that the Jays and Taira had agreed to a five-year deal with an $80MM guarantee and an opt-out after year three. Jeff Passan of ESPN first reported that the deal included a $5MM signing bonus. Photo courtesy of Nick Turchiaro, Imagn Images.

item.title: Padres Re-Sign Garrett Hawkins To Minor League Deal
item.dc:creator: Anthony Franco
item.description: The Padres re-signed reliever Garrett Hawkins on a minor league contract, according to the MiLB.com transaction tracker. San Diego dropped him from the 40-man roster on Friday when they declined to tender him a contract. Hawkins is still seeking to make his big league debut as he enters his age-27 season. A ninth-round draftee in […]
item.content:encoded:
The Padres re-signed reliever Garrett Hawkins on a minor league contract, according to the MiLB.com transaction tracker. San Diego dropped him from the 40-man roster on Friday when they declined to tender him a contract.

Hawkins is still seeking to make his big league debut as he enters his age-27 season. A ninth-round draftee in 2021, Hawkins moved to the bullpen in his fifth minor league season and appeared to have a breakout showing. He combined for a 1.50 ERA across 60 innings between High-A and Double-A in 2025, leading the Friars to add him to their roster last winter to avoid losing him in the Rule 5 draft.

The Canadian righty had a much tougher season in 2026. Hawkins split the year between Double-A San Antonio and Triple-A El Paso, struggling to a 5.47 earned run average across 54 1/3 frames. He recorded a solid 26.6% strikeout percentage but saw his walk rate climb five points to a near-15% clip. Hawkins had particularly ugly strikeout and walk numbers against Triple-A opposition.

The down year cost Hawkins his roster spot but hasn’t entirely soured the front office on his future. It’s fairly common for teams to drop fringe pre-arbitration players at the tender deadline, as that’s the only time that clubs can cut a player from their 40-man roster without needing to trade them or place them on waivers. A non-tender sends the player directly to free agency and allows them to explore opportunities elsewhere, but they’ll often immediately re-sign with their former team if they’re likely to be limited to minor league offers anyway.

item.title: D-Backs Have Gotten Calls On Eduardo Rodriguez, Merrill Kelly
item.dc:creator: Anthony Franco
item.description: The Diamondbacks have received trade calls on starters Eduardo Rodriguez and Merrill Kelly, report Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon of The Athletic. It’s unclear how willing the Snakes are to part with one of their veteran pitchers. Arizona would presumably be more inclined to listen on Kelly, who’s coming off a rough year. Rodriguez was the […]
item.content:encoded:
The Diamondbacks have received trade calls on starters Eduardo Rodriguez and Merrill Kelly, report Ken Rosenthal and Will Sammon of The Athletic. It’s unclear how willing the Snakes are to part with one of their veteran pitchers.

Arizona would presumably be more inclined to listen on Kelly, who’s coming off a rough year. Rodriguez was the team’s best starter in 2026. It’d be easier for the Diamondbacks to find a taker for the lefty, yet that’d subtract from a rotation that already looks shaky. Both pitchers also have limited no-trade protection that’d allow them some say over their destination even if the Diamondbacks look to move them.

Rodriguez is slated to make a $19MM salary next season. He’s also guaranteed a $6MM buyout on an $18MM mutual option that would vest if he throws 110 1/3 innings (and climbs to $19MM if he reaches 160 1/3 frames). Kelly is owed a $21MM salary in the second season of his two-year contract. He’d lock in a $12MM salary for 2028 if he reaches 170 innings next season and would also be owed a $500K assignment bonus from his new team if he’s traded.

There’s probably some surplus value with Rodriguez even as he enters his age-34 season. The southpaw is coming off a seventh place finish in NL Cy Young balloting after turning in a 2.89 earned run average across 32 starts. Rodriguez only struck out 18.1% of opposing hitters with a modest 9.5% swinging strike rate, so it’s unlikely teams will view him as highly as the ERA would suggest. Estimators like FIP (3.89), xERA (4.27) and SIERA (4.62) put his 2026 performance closer to league average.

Rodriguez had the same velocity and a similar strikeout and walk profile in 2025, when he allowed an ERA north of 5.00 across 29 starts. As MLBTR’s Charlie Wright examined last month, his success was driven by excellent command and limiting hard contact. That’s a tougher profile to sustain than if Rodriguez were overpowering hitters, but there’d surely be clubs that view him as a mid-rotation arm who’d be in the mix for a potential playoff start. The difficulty for the Snakes is in both shedding the contract and finding a worthwhile return at a time when they’re still aiming to compete for a playoff spot themselves.

Kelly’s contract is underwater and would require Arizona to eat some of the money or take back another team’s bloated deal. He’s 38 years old coming off a 4.94 ERA across 162 innings. Kelly’s 16.1% strikeout rate was down six percentage points relative to 2025. He allowed a career-high 28 home runs. Kelly had a decent final few weeks but overall looked more like an innings-eating fifth starter than the mid-rotation arm he’s been for most of his big league career.

Arizona’s rotation depth is a concern with Michael Soroka hitting free agency. Rodriguez and Brandon Pfaadt are penciled into two spots. Corbin Burnes will be in there if healthy but has barely pitched over the past season and a half between elbow surgery and a shoulder strain. Recent trade pickup Johan Oviedo has even more durability questions, while Ryne Nelson had an ERA close to 5.00 and missed half the season to a flexor strain.

item.title: Mariners, Carlos Santana Agree To Minor League Deal
item.dc:creator: Anthony Franco
item.description: The Mariners are in agreement with veteran first baseman Carlos Santana on a minor league contract, reports Will Sammon of The Athletic. The Octagon client will get an invite to MLB Spring Training, writes Adam Jude of The Seattle Times. Santana’s career continues for his age-41 season. It’s his second stint in Seattle, as the switch-hitter […]
item.content:encoded:
The Mariners are in agreement with veteran first baseman Carlos Santana on a minor league contract, reports Will Sammon of The Athletic. The Octagon client will get an invite to MLB Spring Training, writes Adam Jude of The Seattle Times.

Santana’s career continues for his age-41 season. It’s his second stint in Seattle, as the switch-hitter spent the second half of the 2022 campaign in the Pacific Northwest. He clearly made a strong impression on the coaching staff and front office. The M’s showed interest in Santana as a free agent over the 2023-24 offseason and reportedly offered him a two-year contract the following winter. Santana declined to take a one-year deal back in Cleveland, where he began his career.

The Mariners are one of nine teams for which Santana has suited up at the MLB level. His most recent big league work was an eight-game stint with the Diamondbacks this past April. Santana limped to a 2-24 start to the season before suffering a right adductor strain that sent him to the injured list for two months. The D-Backs released him once he was healthy rather than find a spot for him on the active roster.

Santana signed a minor league contract with the Braves, appearing in 27 games with their top affiliate in Gwinnett. He batted .292/.385/.382 in that limited look. Santana still draws plenty of walks and is difficult to strike out, but he’s one of the slowest players in the league and isn’t going to hit for a high average on balls in play. Santana hit .219/.308/.325 in his most recent extended big league action in 2025. He has continued to grade as an above-average defensive first baseman deep into his career, aside from subpar marks in an exceedingly tiny sample in Arizona this year.

The Mariners have Josh Naylor locked into the everyday first base role. Santana would provide plenty of experience in a depth role at Triple-A Tacoma if he doesn’t win a job as a bench player and veteran clubhouse presence.

item.title: Reds To Re-Sign Tyler Stephenson To Three-Year Deal
item.dc:creator: Anthony Franco
item.description: The Reds are re-signing free agent catcher Tyler Stephenson on a three-year, $30MM contract, reports Jeff Passan of ESPN. The deal also allows Stephenson, an ACES client, to opt out after the second season. The signing is pending a physical. Cincinnati has a couple openings on the 40-man roster and will not need to make […]
item.content:encoded:
The Reds are re-signing free agent catcher Tyler Stephenson on a three-year, $30MM contract, reports Jeff Passan of ESPN. The deal also allows Stephenson, an ACES client, to opt out after the second season. The signing is pending a physical. Cincinnati has a couple openings on the 40-man roster and will not need to make any corresponding moves.

Cincinnati’s first-round pick in 2015, Stephenson has played his entire career with the Reds. He made a brief debut during the pandemic season and has been the team’s primary catcher over the past six years. Stephenson lost decent chunks of the 2022 and ’25 campaigns to various injuries but has reached 130+ games in the other four of his six full big league seasons.

The righty-swinging Stephenson has developed into a solid bat-first catcher. He’s a lifetime .257/.335/.422 hitter in just shy of 2500 career plate appearances. That’s five points better than league average, as measured by wRC+, at a position where many teams live without much offense. Stephenson has hit between 13 and 19 home runs in each of the past four seasons and carries a .245/.327/.424 slash line since the start of 2024. That puts him in the middle third of starting catchers around the league offensively.

It was essentially more of the same for Stephenson in his walk year. He started very slowly, caught fire for three months between June and August, then slumped again in September. The end result was a league average .241/.323/.404 slash with 15 longballs across 468 plate appearances. He walked at a solid 10.5% clip against a lofty 27.4% strikeout rate.

There’s more of a split on Stephenson’s work behind the plate. No catcher was behind the dish for more stolen bases this past season. His 19% success rate in throwing out baserunners was four percentage points below the league mark, while Statcast had him in the bottom third of MLB in average pop time.

Stephenson rarely commits passed balls and has graded as one of the best blockers in the game over the last couple seasons. However, his pitch framing metrics are routinely well below-average, though this year’s introduction of the ABS challenge system might mitigate that deficiency for catchers. Only William Contreras successfully overturned more called balls than Stephenson did (93) this past season. Some of that is a volume statistic — they were also the top two in challenge attempts — but Stephenson flipped calls at a solid 68% rate.

It’s early enough in the ABS era that teams may have differing ideas on how much to value catchers’ challenge grades. The Reds seemingly didn’t find robust interest when they entertained trading Stephenson at the deadline. The Yankees, in particular, were known to be in the market for a right-handed hitting catcher but reportedly balked at Stephenson’s receiving metrics. The Reds clearly don’t find that to be as big an issue. They’re familiar with his work as a game-caller and clubhouse presence.

Stephenson and Carson Kelly were the two remaining unsigned starting-caliber catchers once Ryan Jeffers accepted a qualifying offer from Minnesota. The Reds needed to do something behind the plate, as they’d been down to Jose Trevino and Will Banfield as the only catchers on the 40-man roster. It’s sensible that they wanted to bring Stephenson back, though the price they paid to do so comes as a bit of a surprise.

MLBTR predicted Stephenson for a more modest two-year, $15MM contract. He instead becomes just the fifth free agent catcher this decade to command a three-year guarantee (as shown on MLBTR’s Contract Tracker). J.T. Realmuto has gotten there twice on his successive contracts with the Phillies. James McCann, Willson Contreras, and Christian Vázquez are the only other free agent catchers since 2020 to sign for three-plus years. Stephenson is the only member of that group to also get an opt-out clause.

Cincinnati will roll with a Stephenson-Trevino pairing behind the dish for a third straight season. Their ill-advised $11.5MM extension with Trevino comes off the books after next season. The organization’s top prospect, 20-year-old catcher Alfredo Duno, reached Double-A at the end of this year. He’ll be added to the 40-man roster a year from now and could take over the primary catching job in 2028. Stephenson would still be under contract for another two seasons at that point, though he could move into a part-time catcher/designated hitter role once Duno arrives.

This is the first notable move of the offseason for the Reds, who entered the day with a projected $89.3MM payroll (courtesy of MLBTR contributor Ethan Hullihen). They opened the ’26 season a little north of $126MM. Gordon Wittenmyer of The Cincinnati Enquirer wrote that Reds’ ownership hadn’t given the front office a budget for next season as of the GM Meetings a couple weeks ago — contributing to their decision not to beat Detroit’s offer to sign closer Emilio Pagán for $11.5MM. It seems they’re operating with clearer guidelines now and were wiling to commit a $10MM average annual value to address their catching need.

It’s one of many areas which president of baseball operations Nick Krall and his group need to address. The Reds have two unproven young players (Carlos Jorge and Héctor Rodríguez) penciled into their starting outfield. They could use a multi-positional infielder to challenge Matt McLain, Juan Brito and Ke’Bryan Hayes for playing time between second and third base. They’ll need at least one back-end reliever to replace Pagán and should be in the market for a rotation upgrade over free agent Brady Singer.

Image courtesy of Aaron Doster, Imagn Images.

item.title: Latest On Adrian Morejon’s Market
item.dc:creator: Anthony Franco
item.description: With Trevor Rogers coming off the board last night, Adrian Morejon is the only unsigned pitcher who is still attached to the qualifying offer. The star setup man reportedly plans to remain in the bullpen despite getting calls from teams interested in building him up as a starter. There hasn’t been a ton of reporting about the […]
item.content:encoded:
With Trevor Rogers coming off the board last night, Adrian Morejon is the only unsigned pitcher who is still attached to the qualifying offer. The star setup man reportedly plans to remain in the bullpen despite getting calls from teams interested in building him up as a starter.

There hasn’t been a ton of reporting about the teams involved in Morejon’s bidding. The Marlins were linked to the Cuban-born southpaw a couple weeks ago but would be a very surprising landing spot for a pitcher who could command a $75-100MM guarantee. The Yankees were also tied to Morejon a few weeks ago, yet that preceded David Bednar surprisingly accepting the $23.15MM qualifying offer. New York has also agreed to a two-year, $18MM deal with Jonathan Loáisiga while finalizing cheaper one-year contracts for southpaws Tim Hill and Brent Suter.

The Yankees already have one of the better lefty relievers in the American League in Brent Headrick. That gives them five relievers already locked into bullpen spots, to say nothing of the likelihood that some of their depth starters (e.g. Clarke Schmidt, Ryan Weathers) might be pushed into relief. Between the team’s pitching depth and their sizable commitments to Bednar and Loáisiga, it’d seem like Morejon is a long shot to wind up in the Bronx. That said, Jon Heyman of The New York Post reported this afternoon that the Yankees remained in the bidding for free agency’s best reliever.

Another AL East club is also in the mix. Mitch Bannon of The Athletic reported on Tuesday that the Blue Jays were engaged on Morejon. That report preceded their agreement with right-hander Kaima Taira on a five-year, $80MM deal this evening. Perhaps that reduces Toronto’s urgency to spend big on another pitcher given their need for a bat, but Taira is surely going to get an opportunity to start. The Jays have a couple high-end righty relievers at the back of the bullpen in Louis Varland and Tyler Rogers. They’re much lighter from the left side, where Mason Fluharty (a pure lefty specialist) is their only reliable option.

Toronto and New York both exceeded the luxury tax threshold this year. They’d both forfeit their second- and fifth-highest draft choices, plus $1MM from their international bonus pools, to sign a qualified free agent.

There is at least one big-market Eastern division team that doesn’t appear to be strongly involved. Matt Gelb and Charlotte Varnes of The Athletic write that the Phillies are not believed to be serious suitors for Morejon. Philadelphia is light on lefty relief and could use another setup option to pair with Jonathan Bowlan in front of star closer Jhoan Duran. They arguably have bigger needs in the corner outfield and at third base than splurging on a reliever, however.

item.title: White Sox To Sign Tyrone Taylor
item.dc:creator: Darragh McDonald
item.description: The White Sox and free agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor have reportedly agreed to a contract worth $17MM over two years. Taylor is represented by THE·TEAM. The Sox have an open 40-man spot at the moment and therefore won’t need a corresponding move to make this deal official. Taylor, 33 in January, has a long track […]
item.content:encoded:
The White Sox and free agent outfielder Tyrone Taylor have reportedly agreed to a contract worth $17MM over two years. Taylor is represented by THE·TEAM. The Sox have an open 40-man spot at the moment and therefore won’t need a corresponding move to make this deal official.

Taylor, 33 in January, has a long track record as a strong defender. In over 4,000 innings on the grass, including time in all three slots, he has been credited with 42 Defensive Runs Saved, 22 Outs Above Average and a mark of 24 from Fielding Run Value. Isolating his work up the middle, it’s over 2,000 innings in center with 17 DRS, 10 OAA and 15 FRV.

Offensively, his résumé is more mixed. He had some good years with the Brewers early on. Through the end of the 2022 season, he had stepped to the plate 729 times and produced a .241/.303/.453 line. That led to a 106 wRC+, indicating he was 6% above league average at the plate overall. His performance dipped in 2023 and he got flipped to the Mets, which didn’t help. From 2023 to 2025, he hit a combined .235/.284/.384 for an 84 wRC+.

His stock was down going into 2026 but the Mets tendered him an arbitration contract, agreeing to a $3.8MM salary for this year. That turned out to be a good decision as Taylor had a strong bounceback campaign. The Mets as a whole were not performing well and went into seller mode at the deadline. They flipped Taylor and Clay Holmes to the Cubs for prospect Jefferson Rojas. The Mets and Cubs mostly used Taylor in a part-time role, as he only got 241 plate appearances on the year, but he hit .279/.325/.502 in those for a 127 wRC+.

Taylor is a right-handed bat and has fared better against southpaws in his career. The Cubs mostly used him in a platoon with Ian Happ after the trade. He hit .239/.303/.431 for a 102 wRC+ against righties this year, though with an unlucky .244 batting average on balls in play. Against lefties, he slashed .318/.348/.573 for a 153 wRC+, though with a very fortunate .349 BABIP.

It’s possible Taylor’s offensive profile is not as extreme as those splits would suggest. As noted, the BABIP luck was with him when he had the platoon advantage but not the rest of the time. For his career, he has a .256/.309/.435 line and 105 wRC+ against lefties, compared to a .236/.290/.420 line and 94 wRC+ the rest of the time.

It’s a profile that fits the current White Sox roster. The Sox project to have Sam Antonacci, Tristan Peters and Braden Montgomery in their outfield next year. Antonacci and Peters are both lefty hitters who have struggled against southpaws thus far. Montgomery is a switch-hitter who was much better against righties in his rookie season.

The Sox acquired Brenton Doyle from the Rockies at the deadline a few months ago. He’s another righty-hitting outfielder with a strong defensive reputation and better numbers against southpaws. It’s a bit redundant to have both Doyle and Taylor on the same roster but it gives manager Will Venable more chances to play matchups in the outfield. Doyle and Taylor could start against lefties while two of the Antonacci/Peters/Montgomery trio head to the bench.

With a righty starter, Doyle and Taylor could be available for pinch-hitting and defensive replacement duties. The Sox also have other lefty bats in the mix, such as Andrew Benintendi, Colson Montgomery, Munetaka Murakami and Kyle Teel, creating even more pinch-hit opportunities. Given Taylor’s age and inconsistency, it’s a bit surprising to see him land a two-year guarantee but he makes a good amount of sense for what’s going on at Rate Field.

The Sox have been trying to upgrade an exciting young team that surprised the baseball world with a postseason run in 2026. Ideally, Taylor helps paper over some of the holes in the position player group. The Sox have added Dustin May to the rotation, though they also subtracted from that part of the roster by dealing Davis Martin and Luis Castillo to the Rockies, using Martin’s trade value as a means of clearing Castillo’s salary. The Sox still want to add to the rotation, so perhaps that will be their next target.

MLBTR’s Payroll Tracker from contributor Ethan Hullihen projects the Sox for a payroll of $100MM next year. Taylor’s deal will probably add about $8-9MM to that, depending on the annual breakdown. That’s already beyond this year’s $99MM payroll but the Sox have been way higher than that in the past, so they should have some powder dry.

Jon Heyman of The New York Post first reported that Taylor was headed to the White Sox. Mark Feinsand of MLB.com first reported the financial details. Photos courtesy of David Banks, Gregory Fisher, Imagn Images

item.title: Multiple Teams Showing Interest In Tyler Austin
item.dc:creator: Darragh McDonald
item.description: Free agent first baseman Tyler Austin is generating interest from multiple clubs, reports Joel Sherman of The New York Post. He lists the Mets, Yankees, Cubs, Blue Jays and Rays as the teams in the mix. Austin, 35, would be a buy-low addition for any club and Sherman notes he would almost certainly have to […]
item.content:encoded:
Free agent first baseman Tyler Austin is generating interest from multiple clubs, reports Joel Sherman of The New York Post. He lists the Mets, Yankees, Cubs, Blue Jays and Rays as the teams in the mix.

Austin, 35, would be a buy-low addition for any club and Sherman notes he would almost certainly have to settle for a minor league deal. He played in the majors from 2016 to 2019. He showed off some power in that time but struck out in 36.9% of his plate appearances.

He then went overseas and revitalized his career with the Yokohama DeNA BayStars of Japan’s Nippon Professional Baseball. He hit 48 home runs over the 2020 and 2021 seasons. The next two campaigns were largely wiped out by injuries but he got back on track in 2024, hitting another 25 home runs. Right knee issues limited him to 65 games in 2025 but he was able to add another 11 homers. Over that six-year stretch from 2020 to 2025, he had a .293/.377/.568 line for the BayStars with a manageable 22.8% strikeout rate.

The Cubs decided to bet on that a year ago, giving Austin a major league deal worth $1.25MM. The plan was seemingly to have Austin serve as a right-handed complement to their lefties, including first baseman Michael Busch. That plan quickly failed, as Austin required a debridement procedure on the patellar tendon in his right knee in February. He missed the entire season. The Cubs outrighted him off the roster at season’s end. Sherman notes that Austin is now healthy.

Though clubs may be intrigued by his big power showing in Japan, his age and injury track record will limit him to minor league offers. For the Cubs, they still have Busch at first base and also added another big lefty bat today by agreeing to a deal with Teruaki Sato. If they can reunite with Austin on a minor league deal, they could get a look at him in spring training. If he’s healthy and playing well, he could perhaps earn a bench spot and help the Cubs play matchups.

For the Mets, they just added righty-swinging Paul Goldschmidt to platoon with lefty Jared Young. Sherman suggests the Goldschmidt signing could push Mark Vientos, another righty bat, off the roster. Bringing Austin aboard on a minor league deal would allow the Mets to effectively replace Vientos without using a roster spot, giving them cover for the event of a Goldschmidt injury.

The Yankees have a couple of lefties, Ben Rice and Luis García Jr., as options for first base and designated hitter. Giancarlo Stanton hits from the right side and could complement those two, though he has a very checkered injury history, so it makes sense that the Yankees would think about having backup plans.

The Jays have Vladimir Guerrero Jr., a righty bat, at first base. Their designated hitter spot is open with the free agency of George Springer. It’s possible switch-hitter Anthony Santander ends up taking a good chunk of the DH at-bats. Toronto has lefties like Brett Bateman, Nathan Lukes, Andrés Giménez, Sean Keys, Josh Smith, Yohendrick Piñango and RJ Schreck elsewhere on the roster so perhaps there’s a scenario where Austin could pinch-hit against tough southpaws while occasionally giving Guerrero a breather at first.

The Rays have lefty Jonathan Aranda at first base and he has pretty notable splits. He has a .283/.362/.470 line and 133 wRC+ against righties compared to a .245/.341/.327 line and 94 wRC+ against southpaws. Ryan Vilade could serve as Aranda’s platoon partner but there would be no harm in having Austin aboard in a non-roster capacity as a fallback plan.

Photo courtesy of Rick Scuteri, Imagn Images

item.title: Tigers Interested In Bryan Abreu
item.dc:creator: Darragh McDonald
item.description: The Tigers are interested in free agent reliever Bryan Abreu, reports Evan Petzold, though Petzold notes that the two sides are currently at an impasse because Abreu is looking for a multi-year deal while the club would prefer to keep an arrangement to one year. Abreu, 30 in April, has a very strong track record […]
item.content:encoded:
The Tigers are interested in free agent reliever Bryan Abreu, reports Evan Petzold, though Petzold notes that the two sides are currently at an impasse because Abreu is looking for a multi-year deal while the club would prefer to keep an arrangement to one year.

Abreu, 30 in April, has a very strong track record but is coming off a down year. From 2022 to 2025, he tossed 281 2/3 innings for the Astros with a 2.30 earned run average. His 10.4% walk rate in that time was a bit high but he punched out 34.3% of batters faced. Among MLB pitchers who logged at least 240 innings in that four-year window, Abreu’s strikeout rate was the very best. He earned 15 saves and 95 holds in that time.

But as mentioned, 2026 was a challenge for him. His 3.73 ERA wasn’t disastrous but he danced around some serious control issues. He walked 41 of the 268 batters he faced, an awful 15.3% clip. He also hit five batters, meaning 17.1% of opponents got a free trip to first base. He uncorked seven wild pitches to boot.

He did rein things in a bit after an atrocious start. Through 11 1/3 innings, he had walked 26.2% of batters faced. By the time he was up to 20 1/3 innings on the year, his walk rate was still all the way up at 23.5% and he had a 7.52 ERA. He then had a strong 1.91 ERA the rest of the way while walking 10.2% of opponents in his final 42 1/3 innings. That walk rate was above average but in line with Abreu’s dominant seasons.

On the heels of that campaign, it makes Abreu difficult to value as a free agent. One year ago, he felt like a guy who could get a deal in the $50-100MM range. But after such a wobbly season, would a club bet on that? MLBTR predicted Abreu to secure a two-year, $22MM deal but with an opt-out halfway through. That would give him the chance to post a better platform season and then return to free agency. The second year would give him a safety net for more struggles or an injury.

For the Tigers, it’s not a surprise that they are interested. They have already added one arm to their bullpen, signing Emilio Pagán last week. After that signing, president of baseball operations Scott Harris said the club would remain on the lookout for further bullpen upgrades.

Signing Abreu and getting the peak 2022 to 2025 version of him would certainly make the Tigers better but the same could be said of just about every club. Some teams have stronger bullpens than others but a relief group goes eight arms deep, so most clubs could add Abreu to bump out their eighth-best guy and come out ahead.

It’s understandable that the Tigers might prefer to keep the commitment to one year, just in case some of Abreu’s struggles carry over into 2027. However, Abreu’s track record should lead to interest from a number of clubs, so some team will probably have to give him multiple years and perhaps an opt-out to get the deal over the line.

Photo courtesy of Vincent Carchietta, Imagn Images

item.title: Mets, Eddys Leonard Agree To Minor League Deal
item.dc:creator: Steve Adams
item.description: The Mets and infielder Eddys Leonard are in agreement on a minor league deal with an invitation to major league spring training, reports Will Sammon of The Athletic. Leonard, 26, made his big league debut with the Giants this past season. He only tallied eight plate appearances, but that was enough time for him to […]
item.content:encoded:
The Mets and infielder Eddys Leonard are in agreement on a minor league deal with an invitation to major league spring training, reports Will Sammon of The Athletic.

Leonard, 26, made his big league debut with the Giants this past season. He only tallied eight plate appearances, but that was enough time for him to get on the board with the first two knocks of his major league career: a single and a double. Leonard spent the remainder of the season in Triple-A between the Giants and Brewers organizations, where he combined to bat .261/.342/.469 while playing six different positions (all four infield spots and both outfield corners). While Leonard has primarily been a shortstop in the minors, he has 800 innings of experience at the hot corner and more than 1300 at second base.

This past season’s Triple-A numbers from Leonard are pretty closely aligned with his career marks. The righty-swinging utilityman has played in parts of four Triple-A seasons and logged a .259/.329/.461 batting line. He’s fanned at just over a 19% clip over the past two seasons (904 plate appearances) and walked at an 8.3% rate.

Leonard joins a crowded infield mix in Queens. The Mets signed Paul Goldschmidt yesterday, ostensibly setting up for a platoon with Jared Young at first base. Brett Baty and Marcus Semien are in the mix at second base. Francisco Lindor and Bo Bichette have the left side of the infield locked down. Jorge Polanco is on hand to mix in at first, second, third and designated hitter. Younger infielders Mark Vientos and Ronny Mauricio are both on the 40-man roster still but are both out of minor league options and feel like offseason change-of-scenery candidates.

item.title: Nationals Among Teams Interested In Jazz Chisholm Jr.
item.dc:creator: Steve Adams
item.description: The Nationals are among the clubs showing interest in free agent infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr., reports Robert Murray of FanSided. There’s no indication a deal is close. Broadly speaking, the market for pitching has moved considerably faster than the market for bats — particularly over the past 72 hours or so (though Teruaki Sato is […]
item.content:encoded:
The Nationals are among the clubs showing interest in free agent infielder Jazz Chisholm Jr., reports Robert Murray of FanSided. There’s no indication a deal is close. Broadly speaking, the market for pitching has moved considerably faster than the market for bats — particularly over the past 72 hours or so (though Teruaki Sato is a notable exception).

Chisholm, 28, is coming off a down season by his standards, although in his case, that still means a 19-homer, 41-steal campaign. The lefty-swinging slugger’s strikeout rate trended in the wrong direction, climbing to nearly 30%, which weighed down his rate stats and left him with a roughly league-average .231/.312/.399 batting line. Defensive metrics, which can vary wildly from season-to-season but tend to offer a reasonably accurate perspective in larger samples, were all over the place in 2026 (-6 DRS, +13 Outs Above Average). Broadly speaking, Defensive Runs Saved has pegged Chisholm as a roughly average second baseman over the past few years, whereas Statcast’s Outs Above Average has him considerably above that threshold.

The fit with the Nationals would register as something of a surprise. Even on the back of a “down” year, Chisholm should have substantial earning power. The Nationals have generally spent at bottom-of-the-scale levels in recent offseasons as an increasingly lengthy rebuild continues to play out slower than hoped. As MLBTR’s Contract Tracker shows, they’ve only given out three multi-year deals in the past half decade — all $14MM or less in total — and have only once gone to an annual value north of $9MM: Nelson Cruz’s one-year, $15MM deal back in 2022. Chisholm would is in a tier of free agents that the Nats simply haven’t touched in recent memory.

Exactly where Chisholm would play in D.C. is an open question. The Nationals began to get longtime shortstop CJ Abrams some work at second base late in the 2026 season, recognizing that Abrams’ glovework at shortstop has graded among the worst in the league. Chisholm himself would be a stretch to return to shortstop. He’s reportedly signaled a willingness to play in the infield and/or in the outfield, which helps his case, but it’s been two years since he played center field for the Marlins. The Nats don’t have a set option at third base, so Chisholm could fit there if Washington brass isn’t concerned with the idea of blocking Brady House. It’s also at least possible that the Nats could get a massive offer for Abrams, who’s down to two years of club control remaining, but they’ve signaled a desire to hang onto him after a career-best performance in 2026.

As things stand, MLBTR contributor Ethan Hullihen has the Nationals projected for far and away the lowest payroll in baseball, at just over $52MM. That’s nearly $22MM behind the 29th-ranked Cardinals and $27MM behind the 28th-ranked Marlins. They’re obviously going to spend some money this winter, whether via signing free agents, acquiring contracts via trade, or a combination of the two. Washington has also hammered out extensions for starter Cade Cavalli and for center fielder Jacob Young over the past three-plus months, further signaling some willingness to spend.

Chisholm has thus far drawn reported interest from the Blue Jays and Padres. The Twins are known to be looking for help at second or first base. The Pirates have a potential opening at second base, depending on what happens with free agent Brandon Lowe, who rejected a $23.15MM qualifying offer from Pittsburgh. The Blue Jays, Angels, A’s and Rays are just a few of the teams that could look to add at second base, and Chisholm could draw interest from a far broader range of teams if he’s willing to play other positions and considered a viable option at said positions in the eyes of a few more clubs.

item.title: Astros To Hire Nate Irving As Assistant Hitting Coach
item.dc:creator: Charlie Wright
item.description: New Astros manager Brad Ausmus’ staff continues to come together. Houston is expected to hire Nate Irving as an assistant hitting coach, reports Joel Sherman of the New York Post. Irving was most recently a hitting coach in the Mets’ minor league system. Irving is the latest addition in what has become an offseason of […]
item.content:encoded:
New Astros manager Brad Ausmus’ staff continues to come together. Houston is expected to hire Nate Irving as an assistant hitting coach, reports Joel Sherman of the New York Post. Irving was most recently a hitting coach in the Mets’ minor league system.

Irving is the latest addition in what has become an offseason of turnover for the Astros. They added J.P. Martinez as pitching coach and Aaron Bates as hitting coach yesterday. The club also hired Bobby Wilson as bench coach last week. Ausmus is taking over for Joe Espada, who was let go at the end of the year. Randy Flores was hired as the new general manager, replacing Dana Brown. He brought former Cardinals colleague Matt Bayer with him as AGM.

After a brief college coaching career, Irving was hired as the Reds bullpen catcher in 2019. Cincinnati moved him to a minor league bench coach position in 2022. Irving got his first gig as a hitting coach in 2023 at the Rookie ball level. He moved up to Single-A the following year.

The Mets hired Irving as their Double-A hitting coach in 2025. He was bumped up to Triple-A this past season. Irving will work with fellow new addition Bates in Houston. The Astros haven’t officially announced they’re moving on from hitting coach Victor Rodriguez, so he could also be in the mix. Assistant hitting coach Anthony Iapoce took a job with the Reds.

Photo courtesy of Sam Greene, Imagn Images

item.title: Tigers To Sign Ha-Seong Kim
item.dc:creator: Darragh McDonald
item.description: The Tigers and infielder Ha-Seong Kim have agreed to a one-year, $5MM deal, reports Jeff Passan of ESPN. The Boras Corporation client can earn an extra $1MM via incentives, per Jon Heyman of The New York Post. Detroit has a full 40-man roster and will need to make a corresponding move once this becomes official. […]
item.content:encoded:
The Tigers and infielder Ha-Seong Kim have agreed to a one-year, $5MM deal, reports Jeff Passan of ESPN. The Boras Corporation client can earn an extra $1MM via incentives, per Jon Heyman of The New York Post. Detroit has a full 40-man roster and will need to make a corresponding move once this becomes official.

It’s a buy-low move for the Tigers, as Kim has battled injuries and underperformed for the past two years but was quite good before that. Kim started his career in the KBO League in South Korea then signed with the Padres ahead of the 2021 season. His first campaign in San Diego was fairly unremarkable but he got into a good groove after that.

From 2022 to 2024, he got into 423 games and stepped to the plate 1,678 times. His 11% walk rate and 17.9% strikeout rate were both a few ticks better than average. He slashed a combined .250/.336/.385 for a 106 wRC+ over that span. He also stole 72 bases and got good grades for his glovework at shortstop, second base and third base. FanGraphs considered the whole package to be worth 10.5 wins above replacement over those three years.

Towards the end of the 2024 season, Kim tore the labrum in his right shoulder and required surgery. He was set to open the 2025 campaign on the injured list. His stock was still high enough that he was able to get a two-year, $29MM deal from the Rays with the second year being a player option.

He eventually recovered from the shoulder surgery and made it back to the field in the summer of 2025 but his performance was inconsistent and he also hit the injured list with some back inflammation. Tampa put him on waivers and Atlanta claimed him. Kim finished the year with a .234/.304/.345 line and 83 wRC+ in 191 plate appearances.

Despite that down year, Kim still felt his market was strong enough that he could turn down his $16MM player option for 2026, the second season of the deal he initially signed with the Rays. He was able to come out ahead by signing a one-year, $20MM deal with Atlanta, with that club hoping for better health and a bounceback.

That plan quickly got derailed. In January, about a month after the new deal was signed, Kim suffered a hand injury when he slipped on some ice in his home country. He tore a tendon in his right middle finger and required surgery. He was on the IL until May and then struggled after being activated. Inflammation in that finger put him back on the IL for roughly another month in July/August. He made just 147 plate appearances over the whole season and put up a brutal .116/.219/.140 line in those.

The Tigers are hoping that Kim can get back on track next year with better health. They’re not making a huge gamble on it. The $5MM price point is bench/utility player money. For reference, last offseason, players like Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Miguel Rojas and Enrique Hernández signed in this range. If Kim is a serviceable bench player for the Tigers, it’s a fine enough investment. If Kim returns to form and becomes more of an everyday player, then that’s even better for the club.

Detroit has a lot of moving pieces on the infield. Spencer Torkelson projects as the first baseman. Kevin McGonigle split his time between shortstop and third base this year. Second baseman Gleyber Torres became a free agent at season’s end. Colt Keith is an option to play some third base but he also has experience at second and first. Hao-Yu Lee had a nice debut season at the plate in 2026 while playing the middle infield spots and third base, though he got poor grades for his glovework. Javier Báez and Zach McKinstry are around as multi-positional types. Prospect Max Anderson, who plays second and third base, is now on the 40-man but doesn’t have any big league experience yet.

It’s a fairly jumbled picture but the Tigers can spread playing time around depending on who’s playing well. Some situations might call for a better hitter while others might push the club to prioritize defense. For Kim, he would ideally get back to the form he showed from 2022 to 2024, providing strong glovework and roughly average offense. That should get him fairly regular playing time. If he doesn’t quite get on that track, he could still be useful as a glove-first utility player.

Photo courtesy of Brett Davis, David Frerker, Imagn Images
